Forgiveness is the hardest problem in human society—how do you forgive those who've done wrong to you? And how do you forgive yourself for doing wrong unto others? This is the greatest problem in the human heart, as Homer showed us. When we forgive each other, we rejuvenate the world, changing it from one of destruction into vitality.

Achilles demonstrated this by sacrificing himself and having the courage to forgive Hector. Achilles told Patroclus, "Not only will I give your son back, but I will ensure that you have enough time for a proper funeral." He also promised not to attack Troy during Hector's funeral. This is the beauty of the Iliad: its most shocking and poignant ending.

The question now is how Homer and the Greeks had such wisdom, while we don't today. The answer lies in their different way of thinking compared to ours.

Our brains have two hemispheres: the right, creative and emotional; and the left, logical and analytical. According to Julian James, the right hemisphere receives information from the universe, which the left hemisphere interprets into reality.

Emanuel Kant distinguished between the "noumena," or things in themselves, and the "phenomena," or things as they appear to us. Our brain interacts with the noumena and then filters it back into phenomena using time and space. Hegel also believed that the universe is composed of vibrations.

Applying this theory, our right brain receives these vibrations, and our left brain transforms them into everyday reality. For most of human history, we interpreted these vibrations as gods and spirits, which allowed us to better understand the universe and ourselves. This model provided access to wisdom, such as that of Homer and the Greeks.

Today, however, we have shut off this part by prioritizing science, logic, and materialism over our right brain. This has made us less creative and wise than the ancient Greeks were.
